title: Liver Detoxification, Bilirubin, and Gland Functions
subject: Gastrointestinal System (GAST)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter follows the work the liver and digestive glands do beyond digestion itself. It traces bilirubin from heme to stool and uses that pathway to read jaundice panels, explains how hepatocytes transform drugs and toxins and how that same chemistry injures zone 3 in acetaminophen and carbon tetrachloride poisoning, and links the loss of hepatic synthesis and ammonia disposal to the findings of liver failure. It closes with the protective chemistry of saliva and the way the gallbladder concentrates and releases bile. Board questions usually give a lab panel, an exposure, or a failing organ and ask which step broke; each section is built so you can work back to that step.
prerequisites: Hepatic lobule and acinus, including zones 1 to 3 and portal blood flow (GI anatomy units)
Red cell life span and splenic removal of senescent red cells
Enzyme cofactors NADPH, UDP-glucuronic acid, and glutathione
Starling forces and plasma oncotic pressure
Composition of bile and the enterohepatic circulation of bile salts

connections.how: Hemolysis raises bilirubin production, which explains unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia, high urine urobilinogen, and black pigment gallstones.
Acetaminophen and carbon tetrachloride are the standard models of bioactivation, glutathione depletion, and free radical membrane injury.
The urea cycle in periportal hepatocytes disposes of ammonia, so its failure explains hyperammonemia and hepatic encephalopathy.
Hepatic synthesis and vitamin K-dependent carboxylation of clotting factors explain why the prothrombin time is the earliest marker of synthetic failure.
Secretory IgA, lysozyme, and lactoferrin in saliva are mucosal defenses whose loss in Sjogren syndrome leads to rampant caries.

Bilirubin linked to glucuronic acid by UGT1A1, which makes it water-soluble, excretable in bile, and filterable into urine; it is reported approximately as direct bilirubin.

Enzymatic conversion of a lipophilic drug or toxin into a more polar product that can be excreted in urine or bile.
A family of heme-containing monooxygenases in the smooth endoplasmic reticulum that use NADPH and O2 to carry out most phase I oxidations.
Metabolism of a relatively harmless compound into a reactive, toxic product, such as NAPQI from acetaminophen or the trichloromethyl radical from carbon tetrachloride.
A tripeptide of glutamate, cysteine, and glycine whose thiol group conjugates electrophiles and reduces peroxides inside cells.
A free radical chain reaction that oxidizes polyunsaturated fatty acids in membrane phospholipids and destroys membrane integrity.
Death of hepatocytes around the central vein, the region with the most CYP2E1 and the least oxygen.
Reversible brain dysfunction caused mainly by ammonia and other gut-derived toxins that bypass or overwhelm a failing liver.
Dry mouth from reduced salivary flow, which removes buffering, remineralization, and antimicrobial protection of the teeth.
A hormone released by duodenal and jejunal I cells in response to fat and protein that contracts the gallbladder and relaxes the sphincter of Oddi.

sections.title: The bilirubin pathway from heme to stool and urine

blocks.text: Bilirubin is the end product of heme breakdown. An adult makes about 250 to 350 mg per day, roughly 80% from senescent red cells removed by macrophages of the spleen, liver, and bone marrow, and the rest from ineffective erythropoiesis and other heme proteins such as myoglobin and cytochromes. Each step of the pathway changes the solubility of the pigment, and solubility decides where bilirubin can travel and where it appears when a step fails.
Formation in the macrophage

Heme oxygenase, a microsomal enzyme that uses O2 and NADPH, opens the porphyrin ring of heme in the rate-limiting step of heme breakdown, releasing green biliverdin, ferrous iron that is stored in ferritin or returned to transferrin, and carbon monoxide, which is exhaled. Biliverdin reductase then uses NADPH to reduce biliverdin to yellow unconjugated bilirubin. Internal hydrogen bonds fold this molecule so that its polar groups are hidden, making it nearly insoluble in water. It therefore travels in plasma tightly bound to albumin, which keeps it out of the glomerular filtrate and, normally, out of the brain.
Uptake, conjugation, and excretion in the hepatocyte

At the sinusoid, bilirubin dissociates from albumin and enters the hepatocyte by facilitated transport (the carriers are not fully defined), then binds cytosolic ligandin, a glutathione S-transferase that limits its escape back to blood. In the smooth endoplasmic reticulum, UDP-glucuronosyltransferase 1A1 (UGT1A1) transfers glucuronic acid from UDP-glucuronic acid, forming mainly bilirubin diglucuronide. Conjugation disrupts the internal hydrogen bonds and makes bilirubin water-soluble. Multidrug resistance-associated protein 2 (MRP2), an ATP-dependent pump on the canalicular membrane, then exports it into bile. Export is the rate-limiting step of hepatic bilirubin handling, which is why diffuse hepatocyte injury raises conjugated bilirubin: the injured cell can still conjugate but cannot excrete, and conjugated pigment refluxes into blood.
Fate in the intestine

Conjugated bilirubin is not absorbed by the small intestine. In the terminal ileum and colon, bacterial beta-glucuronidases remove the glucuronides and bacterial reductases convert bilirubin to colorless urobilinogen. Most urobilinogen is oxidized to stercobilin, the brown pigment of stool. A small fraction (about 10 to 20%) is reabsorbed into portal blood; the liver re-excretes most of it, and the remainder is filtered by the kidney and oxidized in urine to yellow urobilin. This small enterohepatic loop is the basis of the urine urobilinogen test.

blocks.text: The newborn is the main physiologic exception. A high red cell mass with a shorter life span, low UGT1A1 activity, and a sterile gut in which mucosal beta-glucuronidase deconjugates bilirubin for reabsorption instead of conversion to urobilinogen together raise unconjugated bilirubin, typically peaking about day 3 to 5. If free unconjugated bilirubin exceeds albumin binding, or a drug such as a sulfonamide displaces it from albumin, the lipid-soluble pigment crosses the blood-brain barrier and stains the basal ganglia (kernicterus).

blocks.predict: A large bruise resolves over two weeks. Predict its color changes and which serum bilirubin fraction, if any, rises.
blocks.explain: Tissue macrophages degrade the heme in place, making green biliverdin and then yellow bilirubin, so the bruise turns from purple-blue to green to yellow. Pigment made there is unconjugated, so any serum rise is in the unconjugated (indirect) fraction.
blocks.check: Formation in the macrophage and the albumin transport step.

sections.title: Reading jaundice panels: hemolytic, hepatocellular, and obstructive

blocks.text: Serum bilirubin is reported as total and direct. Direct bilirubin reacts with the diazo reagent without an accelerator and approximates the conjugated fraction; indirect bilirubin (total minus direct) approximates the unconjugated fraction. Typical adult values are a total of about 0.3 to 1.2 mg/dL with a direct fraction under about 0.3 mg/dL, and jaundice becomes visible, first in the sclerae, above about 2 to 3 mg/dL.

Two urine tests complete the panel. Urine bilirubin appears only when conjugated bilirubin is raised, because unconjugated bilirubin is bound to albumin and not filtered; dark, tea-colored urine with a positive dipstick places the problem in the liver or biliary tree. Urine urobilinogen reflects how much bilirubin reaches the gut and how well the liver reclaims what is reabsorbed. It rises when more bilirubin is made or when injured hepatocytes fail to re-extract it, and it falls toward zero when bile cannot reach the intestine.

In hemolytic (prehepatic) jaundice, production outruns hepatic uptake and conjugation, so unconjugated bilirubin rises, urine bilirubin is absent (acholuric jaundice), and urine urobilinogen rises because more conjugated bilirubin enters the gut. Because a normal liver conjugates a large load, hemolysis alone seldom raises total bilirubin above about 4 to 5 mg/dL. In hepatocellular jaundice, uptake, conjugation, and especially excretion fail together, so both fractions rise and aminotransferases are markedly raised. In obstructive (posthepatic) jaundice, conjugated bilirubin refluxes into blood, little or none reaches the gut, and retained bile induces canalicular and bile duct cells to make and release alkaline phosphatase (ALP) and gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT).

blocks.title: Jaundice by mechanism
rows: Normal liver enzymes; LDH up, haptoglobin down
blocks.caption: Urine bilirubin tells you whether the conjugated fraction is up; urine urobilinogen tells you whether bilirubin is reaching the gut.

blocks.text: Prolonged conjugated hyperbilirubinemia explains a common puzzle: some conjugated bilirubin binds covalently to albumin (delta bilirubin), measures as direct, is not filtered, and clears with the roughly 3-week half-life of albumin, so after an obstruction is relieved the urine clears quickly while scleral icterus fades slowly. Inherited disorders act at single steps and leave other liver tests normal.

blocks.title: Inherited hyperbilirubinemias
rows: Mild jaundice with fasting, illness, or exertion; common and benign
blocks.caption: Defects before conjugation raise unconjugated bilirubin; defects after conjugation raise conjugated bilirubin.

blocks.title: Worked example: localizing jaundice from the panel
blocks.text: A 58-year-old has jaundice, total bilirubin 9 mg/dL with direct 7 mg/dL, dark urine positive for bilirubin, absent urine urobilinogen, clay-colored stools, ALP four times normal, and ALT mildly raised. Step 1: direct makes up most of the total, so the liver is conjugating and the problem lies at or after excretion. Step 2: positive urine bilirubin confirms a raised water-soluble conjugated fraction. Step 3: absent urobilinogen and pale stool mean bilirubin is not reaching the gut, so the flow of bile is blocked. Step 4: high ALP with modest ALT points to bile duct injury rather than hepatocyte necrosis. Conclusion: obstructive jaundice, as from a common bile duct stone or a tumor of the pancreatic head. Hemolysis would instead show indirect predominance, no urine bilirubin, and high urobilinogen.

sections.title: Phase I and phase II biotransformation and acetaminophen toxicity

blocks.text: Lipophilic drugs and toxins cross membranes easily, so the kidney would filter and then reabsorb them almost indefinitely. The liver converts them into polar products that stay in urine or bile. This biotransformation takes place mainly in the smooth endoplasmic reticulum and cytosol of hepatocytes and runs in two phases.

Phase I reactions (oxidation, reduction, and hydrolysis) introduce or expose a functional group such as hydroxyl, amine, or thiol. Most oxidations are done by cytochrome P450 monooxygenases, which receive electrons from NADPH through NADPH-cytochrome P450 reductase and insert one oxygen atom from O2 into the substrate while reducing the other to water. CYP activity can be induced (CYP2E1 by chronic ethanol) or inhibited, which changes how much of any metabolite forms. Phase I products are often only slightly more polar and sometimes more reactive than the parent compound, which is the basis of bioactivation.

Phase II reactions attach a large polar donor group, which usually inactivates the molecule and makes it water-soluble. Glucuronidation has high capacity, sulfation has high affinity but limited capacity and saturates first, and glutathione conjugation captures electrophiles. Glutathione, a tripeptide of glutamate, cysteine, and glycine, is made in the hepatocyte at a rate limited by cysteine supply. Conjugates leave through canalicular and basolateral transporters such as MRP2.

blocks.title: Phase I and phase II biotransformation
rows: Glucuronidation, sulfation, glutathione conjugation, acetylation, methylation
Mostly cytosol; UGTs in endoplasmic reticulum
Small rise in polarity; may become reactive
Large rise in polarity; usually inactive
blocks.caption: Phase I can create a toxic metabolite; phase II usually removes it.

blocks.text: Acetaminophen shows how the two phases balance. At therapeutic doses, most is glucuronidated and sulfated, and only about 5 to 10% is oxidized, mainly by CYP2E1 with contributions from CYP3A4 and CYP1A2, to N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine (NAPQI), an electrophile that glutathione neutralizes at once. In overdose, sulfation and then glucuronidation saturate, more drug flows through CYP oxidation, and glutathione is consumed faster than it is made. When hepatic glutathione falls to roughly 30% of normal, free NAPQI binds cysteine residues on cellular proteins, especially mitochondrial proteins, producing oxidative stress, ATP depletion, and necrosis.

blocks.title: Acetaminophen overdose to zone 3 necrosis
steps: Overdose saturates sulfation, then glucuronidation
More drug is oxidized by CYP2E1 to NAPQI
Glutathione conjugates NAPQI until stores are depleted
Free NAPQI binds cysteine groups on mitochondrial proteins
Oxidative stress and ATP failure cause hepatocyte necrosis
Necrosis concentrates in zone 3 around the central vein
blocks.caption: The toxic step is not the drug itself but the reactive metabolite left over once glutathione is exhausted.

blocks.text: Necrosis is centrilobular (zone 3) because hepatocytes around the central vein hold the most CYP2E1, receive the least oxygenated blood, and have smaller glutathione reserves than periportal cells. Aminotransferases often climb into the thousands of units per liter and peak about 3 to 4 days after ingestion. Chronic alcohol use (CYP2E1 induction and low glutathione) and fasting or malnutrition (low glutathione) lower the toxic threshold. N-acetylcysteine protects because it supplies cysteine for new glutathione, which confirms that glutathione depletion is the critical step.

blocks.predict: Two people take the same large acetaminophen dose. One drinks heavily every day; the other has been fasting for several days. Who is at greater risk, and through which step?
blocks.explain: Both are at higher risk than a healthy person. Chronic drinking induces CYP2E1, so more NAPQI forms, and also lowers glutathione; fasting lowers glutathione and the sulfate and glucuronide donors, so less NAPQI can be neutralized. Either change tips the balance toward free NAPQI.

sections.title: Carbon tetrachloride: free radical injury in the liver

blocks.text: Carbon tetrachloride (CCl4), a former dry-cleaning solvent, is the classic model of free radical injury. CCl4 itself is relatively inert. In the smooth endoplasmic reticulum, CYP2E1 transfers an electron to it, releasing a chloride ion and forming the trichloromethyl free radical (CCl3•). A free radical has an unpaired electron in its outer orbital, which makes it highly reactive and able to start chain reactions.

CCl3• reacts with O2 to form the trichloromethyl peroxyl radical (CCl3OO•). These radicals pull hydrogen atoms from polyunsaturated fatty acids in membrane phospholipids, starting lipid peroxidation. The lipid radicals that result react with O2 to form lipid peroxyl radicals, which attack neighboring fatty acids, so damage spreads autocatalytically through the endoplasmic reticulum membrane until vitamin E or glutathione peroxidase ends the chain. Peroxidation fragments fatty acids into reactive aldehydes, such as malondialdehyde and 4-hydroxynonenal, that cross-link proteins. The radicals also inactivate the cytochrome P450 that produced them.

Fatty change comes first. Within hours, the injured endoplasmic reticulum swells, ribosomes detach, and protein synthesis falls, including synthesis of apolipoproteins. Without apolipoprotein, the hepatocyte cannot package triglyceride into very low density lipoprotein (VLDL) for export, so lipid collects as cytoplasmic vacuoles. Injury then spreads to the plasma membrane and mitochondria. Ca2+ enters through the damaged membrane and activates phospholipases, proteases, and endonucleases, and mitochondrial injury stops ATP production, so the cells swell, lose membrane integrity, and die by necrosis.

The necrosis is centrilobular for the same reason as in acetaminophen injury: CYP2E1 is concentrated in zone 3, where oxygen is lowest. Chronic ethanol use, by inducing CYP2E1, increases CCl4 toxicity, and repeated exposure causes fibrosis, which is why CCl4 is used experimentally to produce cirrhosis. The two toxins differ in the reactive species and in what protects against them.

blocks.caption: A single enzymatic step turns an inert solvent into a radical whose chain reaction does the damage.

blocks.title: Acetaminophen and carbon tetrachloride compared
blocks.caption: Both are bioactivation injuries in zone 3; they differ in the chemistry of the toxic product.

sections.title: Hepatic synthesis, ammonia disposal, and the findings of liver failure

blocks.text: Hepatocytes make most plasma proteins, and portal blood passes through the liver before reaching the systemic circulation, so liver failure produces too little of what the liver makes and too much of what it should remove.
Albumin and clotting factors

Albumin is the most abundant plasma protein (about 3.5 to 5.0 g/dL). The liver makes about 10 to 15 g per day, and its half-life is about 20 days. Albumin supplies roughly 75 to 80% of plasma oncotic pressure, so a low level favors filtration, causing edema and, with portal hypertension and renal Na+ retention, ascites. Because of its long half-life, albumin reflects chronic rather than acute synthetic failure.

The liver makes fibrinogen, prothrombin (factor II), factors V, VII, IX, X, XI, XII, and XIII, the anticoagulants protein C, protein S, and antithrombin, and plasminogen. Factors II, VII, IX, and X and proteins C and S need vitamin K-dependent gamma-carboxylation of glutamate residues to bind Ca2+ and phospholipid. The prothrombin time (PT, about 11 to 13.5 s; INR about 1.0) measures factor VII and the common pathway (X, V, II, fibrinogen). Factor VII has the shortest half-life, about 4 to 6 hours, so the PT lengthens within a day of acute failure and is the earliest marker of synthetic function. In cholestasis the PT is long from vitamin K malabsorption and corrects with parenteral vitamin K; in hepatocellular failure it does not, because synthesis itself has failed. Factor VIII, made mainly by endothelial cells, stays normal or high in liver disease but is consumed in disseminated intravascular coagulation.
Ammonia and the urea cycle

Ammonia comes from colonic bacterial urease, enterocyte glutamine breakdown, and amino acid catabolism. Periportal (zone 1) hepatocytes convert it to urea, and perivenous (zone 3) hepatocytes trap what remains as glutamine. In mitochondria, carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (CPS I), activated by N-acetylglutamate, combines NH3 and HCO3- into carbamoyl phosphate, the committed step; ornithine transcarbamylase forms citrulline, aspartate adds the second nitrogen in the cytosol, and arginase releases urea for renal excretion. Urea cycle failure therefore lowers BUN while raising ammonia.

When hepatocyte mass falls or portosystemic shunts carry portal blood around the liver, ammonia reaches the brain. Astrocytes lack a urea cycle and detoxify it with glutamine synthetase; glutamine accumulates, draws in water, and swells the astrocytes, and neurotransmission is disturbed. Alkalosis shifts NH4+ to freely diffusible NH3, hypokalemia increases renal ammonia production, and gastrointestinal bleeding adds a protein load, so each can precipitate encephalopathy.

blocks.title: Worked example: timing of PT and albumin
blocks.text: Two days after an acetaminophen overdose, a patient has a PT of 28 s and an albumin of 4.1 g/dL. Step 1: factor VII (half-life about 4 to 6 hours) is nearly gone after two days without synthesis, so the PT lengthens sharply. Step 2: albumin (half-life about 20 days) falls well under 10% in two days, so it stays normal. Step 3: a normal albumin does not mean the liver is working. In long-standing cirrhosis both are abnormal, because months of reduced synthesis have lowered albumin.

sections.title: Protective functions of saliva and caries when flow falls

blocks.text: The salivary glands secrete about 1 to 1.5 L per day. The parotid makes serous saliva rich in alpha-amylase, the submandibular a mixed secretion, and the sublingual mostly mucus. Secretion is driven chiefly by parasympathetic fibers (facial nerve to the submandibular and sublingual glands, glossopharyngeal nerve through the otic ganglion to the parotid) acting on M3 muscarinic receptors; sympathetic stimulation adds a smaller, protein-rich flow. Acinar cells secrete an isotonic, plasma-like fluid, and the ducts reabsorb Na+ and Cl- and secrete K+ and HCO3-, so resting saliva is hypotonic. Stimulated flow carries more HCO3-, so buffering capacity is greatest during meals, when acid challenge is highest.

Enamel is mostly hydroxyapatite, a calcium phosphate crystal. After sugar intake, plaque bacteria such as Streptococcus mutans ferment carbohydrate to lactic acid, and plaque pH falls within minutes. Below a critical pH of about 5.5, the fluid around the enamel is undersaturated with hydroxyapatite and mineral dissolves. Saliva reverses this three ways: its flow clears sugar and acid, its bicarbonate (with phosphate and proteins) buffers plaque acid back toward neutral, and because it is supersaturated with calcium and phosphate, mineral redeposits in early lesions once pH recovers (remineralization). Proteins such as statherin keep calcium phosphate in solution without letting it precipitate, and fluoride taken up during remineralization forms fluorapatite, which resists acid better.

blocks.title: Antimicrobial and protective components of saliva
rows: Dimeric IgA from local plasma cells, carried across the epithelium by the polymeric immunoglobulin receptor; blocks bacterial adherence
Hydrolyzes the bond between N-acetylmuramic acid and N-acetylglucosamine in peptidoglycan
Binds iron, depriving bacteria of an essential nutrient
Oxidizes thiocyanate to hypothiocyanite, which inhibits bacterial metabolism
Lubricate and coat the mucosa and aggregate bacteria for swallowing
blocks.caption: These defenses act together with flow, buffering, and remineralization.

blocks.text: Caries form when demineralization outpaces remineralization over time. When flow falls (xerostomia from Sjogren syndrome, radiation to the head and neck, dehydration, or drugs with anticholinergic action that block M3 receptors), sugar and acid stay on the teeth longer, buffering and remineralization fail, and antimicrobial proteins are lost. Caries then progress rapidly and appear at sites that saliva normally protects well, such as the cervical margins at the gumline, exposed root surfaces, and incisal edges. Loss of these defenses also favors oral candidiasis and, with slow flow through the ducts, ascending bacterial parotitis.

sections.title: Gallbladder concentration, contraction, and gallstone formation

blocks.text: The liver secretes about 600 to 1,000 mL of bile per day, but the gallbladder holds only about 30 to 60 mL. Between meals the contracted sphincter of Oddi diverts hepatic bile into the gallbladder, which stores it and concentrates it, usually about 5-fold and up to about 12 to 20-fold.

Concentration is driven by active Na+ transport. Na+ enters the apical membrane in exchange for H+, Cl- enters in exchange for HCO3-, and the basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase pumps Na+ into the lateral intercellular spaces, with Cl- following. The local osmotic gradient draws water across the epithelium, so absorption is nearly isotonic. Bile salts, cholesterol, phospholipid, and bilirubin are large or held in micelles and are not absorbed, so they become concentrated, and the exchange of Na+ for H+ acidifies gallbladder bile, which keeps calcium salts more soluble.

Fatty acids and amino acids in the duodenum stimulate I cells of the duodenal and jejunal mucosa to release cholecystokinin (CCK). CCK acts on CCK1 receptors on gallbladder smooth muscle, and through vagal pathways, to contract the gallbladder, and it relaxes the sphincter of Oddi, so concentrated bile arrives when there is fat to emulsify. Vagal acetylcholine causes modest contraction in the cephalic phase, and the gallbladder partly empties with the migrating motor complex between meals.

Cholesterol is insoluble in water and stays in solution only in mixed micelles with bile salts and phosphatidylcholine. Bile becomes supersaturated when the liver secretes too much cholesterol (obesity, estrogen, aging) or too little bile salt (ileal disease or resection that breaks the enterohepatic circulation). Supersaturation alone is not enough: cholesterol monohydrate crystals must nucleate, a step promoted by mucin from the gallbladder wall, and they must remain long enough to grow. Concentration raises the levels of cholesterol and calcium, and stasis provides the time. Stasis follows fasting and total parenteral nutrition (no fat in the duodenum, so little CCK), pregnancy (progesterone relaxes smooth muscle), rapid weight loss, and spinal cord injury.

blocks.title: Cholesterol gallstone formation
steps: Excess cholesterol or too little bile salt reaches bile
Micelles cannot hold all the cholesterol: supersaturation
Gallbladder absorbs water, concentrating cholesterol and calcium
Low CCK or impaired motility leaves bile stagnant
Mucin promotes nucleation of cholesterol crystals
Crystals aggregate into sludge, then stones
blocks.caption: Stones need supersaturation, nucleation, and stasis together.

blocks.text: Pigment stones follow the same logic for bilirubin. In chronic hemolysis more bilirubin enters bile, some is deconjugated, and unconjugated bilirubin precipitates with calcium as black calcium bilirubinate stones in the gallbladder. In biliary infection, bacterial beta-glucuronidase deconjugates bilirubin in the ducts, forming soft brown stones.

blocks.predict: A patient on total parenteral nutrition for six weeks develops gallbladder sludge. Which step of normal gallbladder function has been lost, and why does that matter?
blocks.explain: With nothing entering the duodenum, I cells release little CCK, so the gallbladder rarely contracts. Bile keeps being concentrated and stays put, giving cholesterol crystals and calcium salts time to nucleate within mucin and form sludge.
blocks.check: The CCK paragraph and the gallstone flow.

integration.text: Anatomy and biochemistry explain where injury lands. Blood enters the acinus at the portal tract and leaves at the central vein, so zone 1 hepatocytes receive the most oxygen and do most urea synthesis, while zone 3 cells, low in oxygen and rich in CYP2E1, take the brunt of bioactivated toxins and of ischemia. The same solubility chemistry links hematology to the liver and gallbladder: hemolysis raises unconjugated bilirubin and urine urobilinogen and can form black pigment stones, while obstruction of the duct that drains a stone-filled gallbladder causes conjugated hyperbilirubinemia with pale stool.

Physiology and pathology explain the lab pattern. Each finding of liver failure traces to a lost function, and the time course follows protein half-lives, so the PT reports acute failure while albumin reports chronic disease. The limits matter too: direct bilirubin only approximates conjugated bilirubin, albumin also falls in malnutrition, nephrotic syndrome, and inflammation, serum ammonia correlates only loosely with the depth of encephalopathy, and reference ranges vary by laboratory, so values are read together rather than one at a time.

summary: Heme oxygenase makes biliverdin, iron, and CO; biliverdin reductase makes unconjugated bilirubin, which rides on albumin and cannot enter urine.
UGT1A1 conjugates bilirubin with glucuronic acid; MRP2 export into bile is rate-limiting; gut bacteria make urobilinogen and stercobilin.
Urine bilirubin means conjugated hyperbilirubinemia; urine urobilinogen rises in hemolysis and disappears in complete obstruction.
Hemolytic jaundice is unconjugated and acholuric; hepatocellular raises both fractions and ALT; obstructive is conjugated with pale stool and high ALP.
Phase I (CYP450, NADPH, O2) adds a reactive group and can bioactivate; phase II conjugation makes products polar and usually inactive.
Acetaminophen overdose saturates conjugation, NAPQI depletes glutathione and binds proteins, and necrosis is centrilobular (zone 3).
CYP2E1 converts CCl4 to the trichloromethyl radical, which drives lipid peroxidation, fatty change from failed VLDL export, and zone 3 necrosis.
The PT (factor VII, half-life about 4 to 6 hours) is the earliest marker of synthetic failure; albumin (about 20 days) reflects chronic disease.
Ammonia normally becomes urea in zone 1; in liver failure it reaches astrocytes, forms glutamine, and causes encephalopathy with asterixis.

Saliva buffers acid, remineralizes enamel, and kills bacteria; xerostomia causes rapid cervical and root caries. The gallbladder concentrates bile by Na+ absorption, contracts with CCK, and forms stones from supersaturation, nucleation, and stasis.

verify: Daily bilirubin production (250 to 350 mg) and the fraction of urobilinogen reabsorbed (about 10 to 20%) differ slightly among sources.
Reference ranges for total and direct bilirubin, PT, INR, and the threshold for visible jaundice (about 2 to 3 mg/dL) vary by laboratory and text.
The statement that hemolysis alone seldom raises total bilirubin above about 4 to 5 mg/dL is a widely taught approximation; confirm the value NABNE uses.
The fraction of acetaminophen oxidized to NAPQI (about 5 to 10%) and the glutathione threshold for injury (about 30% of normal) are approximate and vary by source.
Factor VII half-life is quoted from about 3 to 6 hours and albumin half-life from about 19 to 21 days.
Gilbert syndrome UGT1A1 activity (often quoted as about 30% of normal) and its prevalence vary among sources; confirm whether NABNE expects the UGT1A1 promoter variant detail.
The critical enamel pH is usually given as about 5.5, but values of 5.2 to 5.7 appear in dental texts.
Gallbladder concentrating capacity is quoted as about 5-fold typically and up to 12 to 20-fold; capacity of 30 to 60 mL and hepatic bile output of 600 to 1,000 mL per day follow Guyton and Hall.

The sinusoidal carrier for unconjugated bilirubin uptake is not settled (OATP1B1 is proposed; Rotor syndrome shows OATP1B1 and OATP1B3 mainly reclaim conjugated bilirubin), so the text names facilitated transport only.
Confirm whether NABNE Part I expects transporter names (OATP1B1, OATP1B3, MRP2), the term delta bilirubin, or the CCK1 receptor name, or only the descriptive steps.
